title: Gate-Based Quantum Simulation of Finite-Temperature Open-System Dynamics: A Post-Processing Reconstruction Approach for Collision Models
abstract: Simulating open-system dynamics on gate-based quantum computers offers a route to exploring dissipative quantum phenomena through programmable quantum processing. Collision models provide a direct and flexible framework by representing the environment through sequential system--ancilla collisions. At finite temperatures, however, they typically require repeated preparation of thermal ancillas, adding circuit overhead and gate errors. Here, we show that, for a broad class of $U(1)$-symmetric system--ancilla interactions, finite-temperature dynamics can instead be reconstructed from simulations with pure ancillas in orthogonal basis states. The target temperature enters only through classical post-processing of the resulting pure-branch data, allowing the same data to be reused for different temperatures without additional quantum processing. Bypassing explicit thermal-state preparation reduces ancilla-preparation overhead and preparation-induced errors.
summary: This paper proposes a novel method to simulate open quantum system dynamics at finite temperatures using gate-based quantum computers. By exploiting U(1) symmetry, the authors show that the complex thermal dynamics can be reconstructed classically from measurements performed only with pure ancilla states. This significantly reduces quantum circuit overhead and preparation errors compared to traditional thermal state preparation methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating finite-temperature open-system dynamics on gate-based quantum computers, specifically minimizing the overhead and errors associated with preparing thermal ancilla states.
main_result: It demonstrates that for U(1)-symmetric interactions, finite-temperature dynamics can be reconstructed classically from measurements performed using only pure ancilla states, thereby bypassing explicit thermal state preparation.
method: The methodology involves decomposing the dynamics into population and coherence sectors, deriving reconstruction formulas based on the symmetry constraints, and analyzing the resulting error scaling for different noise models.
model_or_system: The system is an open quantum system modeled using collision maps, where the environment interaction is represented by sequential system-ancilla collisions. The dynamics are analyzed using the Bloch vector representation and exploiting U(1) symmetry.
key_observables: Population relaxation coefficients ($\gamma$), coherence variables ($w$), and preparation-induced error terms ($\Delta r_{	ext{prep}}^n$, $E_{	ext{prep}}^n$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), which is treated classically in the post-processing step; noise parameters associated with the depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels.
main_assumptions: The reconstruction relies critically on the U(1) symmetry of the system-ancilla interactions; error analysis uses first-order approximations in error parameters.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the workflow: generating pure-branch data on the quantum computer followed by classical reconstruction to determine finite-temperature dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the collision model and symmetry decomposition, presents the reconstruction formulae for both population and coherence sectors, and concludes with a detailed comparison of preparation-induced error scaling under various noise models.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, resource-efficient protocol for simulating thermal quantum dynamics on near-term quantum hardware by shifting the complexity from quantum state preparation to classical post-processing.
